subject: paediatrics
title: Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects: Shunts and Auscultation

steps.tx: Acyanotic congenital cardiac defects with left-to-right shunting increase pulmonary blood flow and chamber volume. The most common congenital cardiac malformation in childhood is the **ventricular septal defect** (VSD), comprising twenty-five to thirty percent of all congenital heart disease. Shunt magnitude depends upon the anatomical diameter of the defect and the relative ratio of pulmonary to systemic vascular resistance.
steps.say: Ventricular septal defect is the most common congenital heart lesion, comprising thirty percent of cases. Blood shunts left-to-right from the high-pressure left ventricle into the pulmonary circulation.

right.title: Haemodynamic Determinants
points: Ratio of pulmonary to systemic vascular resistance (PVR:SVR)
Risk of Eisenmenger complex if uncorrected

steps.tx: Defect topography across the interventricular septum influences natural history and spontaneous closure rates. The majority of defects are **perimembranous ventricular septal defects**, accounting for eighty percent of cases, situated in the membranous septum beneath the aortic valve. Muscular defects occur within the trabecular septum and exhibit high spontaneous closure rates, while supracristal outlet defects predispose to progressive aortic valve prolapse and regurgitation.
steps.say: Perimembranous defects comprise eighty percent of VSDs, located beneath the aortic valve. Muscular defects frequently close spontaneously, while outlet defects risk aortic regurgitation.

rows: Moderate closure via tricuspid tissue pouch
Rarely closes; causes aortic valve prolapse

steps.tx: Decreasing neonatal pulmonary vascular resistance over the first two months unmasks left-to-right shunting. As physiological pulmonary vascular resistance drops at six to eight weeks of life, a large VSD precipitates **congestive heart failure in infants**, presenting with tachypnoea, poor feeding, diaphoresis across the forehead during feeds, failure to thrive, and hepatomegaly, secondary to massive pulmonary overcirculation and left ventricular volume overload.
steps.say: Infants develop heart failure at six to eight weeks as pulmonary resistance drops. Symptoms include tachypnoea, head sweating during feeds, poor weight gain, and hepatomegaly.

left.title: Small VSD (Maladie de Roger)
points: Restrictive defect with normal pulmonary pressure
Palpable systolic thrill at left sternal border
Child is entirely asymptomatic with normal growth

right.title: Large Unrestrictive VSD
points: Defect equal to aortic orifice diameter
Softer holosystolic murmur; apical flow rumble
Severe congestive heart failure at 2 months

steps.tx: Auscultation of a ventricular septal defect reflects turbulent systolic jet flow across the interventricular boundary. The clinical hallmark is a **harsh holosystolic murmur**, heard loudest at the left lower sternal border, often accompanied by a systolic thrill. In large shunts, torrential pulmonary venous return traversing the mitral valve generates a soft low-pitched mid-diastolic flow rumble at the cardiac apex.
steps.say: A harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border is the clinical hallmark of a VSD. Large shunts generate an apical mid-diastolic flow rumble across the mitral valve.

steps.tx: Interatrial communication allows left-to-right shunting into the low-pressure right atrium and ventricle. The most frequent variant of **ostium secundum atrial septal defect** accounts for seventy percent of interatrial defects, situated in the central fossa ovalis. Interatrial shunts cause chronic right atrial and right ventricular volume overload with pulmonary plethora, remaining clinically silent throughout early childhood until exertional fatigue emerges.
steps.say: Ostium secundum atrial septal defects involve the fossa ovalis, causing right ventricular volume overload. Children are usually asymptomatic until school age when exertional fatigue appears.

vis.alt: Anatomical progression diagram of interatrial septation, ostium secundum formation, and the fossa ovalis flap valve.
vis.caption: Embryological progression of interatrial septation from septum primum to septum secundum and ostium secundum closure. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Auscultation of an atrial septal defect reveals an unvarying splitting interval of the second heart sound. The pathognomonic physical finding is a **wide fixed split S2**, where the interval between aortic (A2) and pulmonary (P2) valve closure remains wide and does not vary with respiration. Respiratory changes in systemic venous return are cancelled out by reciprocal changes in interatrial shunt volume, maintaining constant right ventricular ejection time.
steps.say: A wide, fixed split second heart sound that does not change with respiration is pathognomonic for an atrial septal defect. Right ventricular ejection time remains constant throughout breathing.

rows: Both components loud and split across cycle
Grade 2/6 ejection murmur at upper LSB
Increased flow across normal pulmonary valve
Murmur arises from valve, not defect
Soft mid-diastolic murmur at lower LSB

steps.tx: Electrocardiographic patterns distinguish secundum from primum interatrial communications. An ostium secundum defect displays **right bundle branch block rSR pattern** with right axis deviation in precordial lead V1, reflecting right ventricular diastolic volume overload. Conversely, an ostium primum defect exhibits marked left axis deviation with counter-clockwise loop inscription, resulting from congenital postero-inferior displacement of the atrioventricular conduction bundle.
steps.say: Secundum ASD shows right axis deviation and an rSR pattern in lead V1. Primum ASD features marked left axis deviation due to displaced cardiac conduction pathways.

left.title: Ostium Secundum ECG Pattern
points: Incomplete right bundle branch block (rSR' in V1)

right.title: Ostium Primum ECG Pattern
points: Extreme left axis deviation (-30 to -90 degrees)

steps.tx: Transcatheter device intervention has replaced open surgical cardiopulmonary bypass for anatomical secundum defects. Modern management deploys **transcatheter amplatzer septal occluder** devices delivered percutaneously through the femoral vein under transoesophageal echocardiography guidance. Candidates require adequate circumferential rims of septal tissue around the defect, whereas ostium primum, sinus venosus, and large unrestrictive perimembranous VSDs mandate open surgical patch closure.
steps.say: Percutaneous Amplatzer device closure is first-line therapy for ostium secundum ASDs with adequate tissue rims. Primum and sinus venosus defects require open surgical patch repair.

rows: >=5 mm margin to coronary sinus and AV valves
Surgical repair of cleft mitral valve
